subtitle: From Chandela dust to UNESCO stone, the long remembering of Khajuraho

panels.shot: split-diagonal composition, one half medieval caravan under a crescent moon, other half Victorian surveyor before vine-clad temples
panels.action: On the left, Ibn Battuta stands beside a small caravan near a looming, half-ruined temple in a moonlit Bundelkhand forest; on the right, T.S. Burt shades his eyes before the same temple now choked in jungle, both men linked by the stone silhouettes.

dialogue.text: Across five centuries, from Ibn Battuta to T.S. Burt, Khajuraho slipped from royal capital to forest shrine to world heritage, enduring mutilation, neglect and rediscovery in quiet Chandela stone.

i18n.hi: पाँच सदियों तक, इब्न बतूता से टी.एस. बर्ट तक, खजुराहो शाही राजधानी से जंगल मंदिर, फिर विश्व विरासत बना, काट-फाड़, उपेक्षा और चुप पुनःखोज झेलता हुआ।

panels.shot: slow push-in on weathered carvings fading into darkness
panels.action: Close on intricate but worn sculptures on a Khajuraho wall, their faces chipped, their bodies softened by time, as shadow from encroaching trees falls across the stone.

dialogue.text: When the Chandela kings were gone and their courts fell silent, their temples did not vanish in a day; they sank slowly, century by century, into another kind of life.

i18n.hi: जब चंदेल राजे गए और दरबार सूने पड़े, मंदिर एक दिन में नहीं ग़ायब हुए; वे सदियों में धीरे-धीरे दूसरी ज़िंदगी में उतर गए।

panels.action: A bird’s-eye view of Bundelkhand in the 14th century shows rocky outcrops, patches of forest, a fort at Kalinjar in the distance, and the clustered spires of Khajuraho rising above trees.

dialogue.text: In the fourteenth century, Bundelkhand lay between powers. Old Chandela strongholds like Kalinjar still watched the plains, and, in the forests, Khajuraho’s towers still caught the sun.

i18n.hi: चौदहवीं सदी में बुंदेलखंड ताकतों के बीच फँसा था। कलिंजर जैसे चंदेल गढ़ अब भी मैदानी इलाकों को निहारते थे, और जंगलों में खजुराहो की मीनारें अब भी धूप पकड़ती थीं।

panels.shot: tracking mid-shot of Ibn Battuta on horseback
panels.action: Ibn Battuta rides a sturdy horse along a dusty path with a small group of companions; he wears a travel-stained robe and turban, his face alert as he looks toward the distant outline of temples.

dialogue.text: Around 1335, the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta crossed this land. His Rihla records a place he called Kajarra, where broken idols and living ascetics shared the same ground.

i18n.hi: करीब 1335 में मोरक्को के यात्री इब्न बतूता ने यह इलाका पार किया। अपनी रिहला में वह जगह ‘कजार्रा’ लिखता है, जहाँ टूटी मूर्तियाँ और जिंदा तपस्वी एक ही धरती बाँटते थे।

panels.shot: low-angle wide of temple front with figures at base
panels.action: A low-angle view shows Ibn Battuta and his Muslim companions at the base of a Khajuraho temple, looking up at towering, sculptured walls where many images have visibly broken faces or missing limbs.

dialogue.text: He writes of idols mutilated by Muslims before him, their noses and faces struck away, yet the bodies still fixed in stone, the temple walls still crowded with carved forms.

i18n.hi: वह लिखता है कि उससे पहले मुस्लिमों ने मूर्तियों की नाक और चेहरे तोड़ दिए थे, पर देहें पत्थर में जमी रहीं, मंदिर दीवारें अब भी नक्काशी से भरी थीं।

panels.shot: medium shot of yogis under a mandapa
panels.action: Under the shade of a pillared mandapa beside the temple, bare-chested yogis sit cross-legged on mats, one in a meditative pose while another speaks calmly to a standing Muslim visitor.

dialogue.text: Near these damaged images, he saw Hindu ascetics. Ibn Battuta notes yogis still practising there, and Muslims coming to learn from them about discipline, breath and renunciation.

i18n.hi: इन घायल मूर्तियों के पास ही उसने हिंदू साधु देखे। इब्न बतूता लिखता है कि योगी अब भी तप करते थे, और मुसलमान उनसे अनुशासन, साँस और त्याग सीखने आते थे।

panels.shot: intimate medium close-up on Ibn Battuta listening
panels.action: Ibn Battuta stands slightly apart, listening intently as a bearded yogi gestures toward his own chest, the temple steps behind them filled with quiet onlookers.

dialogue.speaker: Ibn Battuta
dialogue.text: Their devotion is severe. Our men seek to test their own souls through it.

i18n.hi: उनकी साधना कठोर है। हमारे लोग इसी से अपनी रूह आज़माते हैं।

panels.shot: wide shot transitioning time via split composition
panels.action: The same temple seen from the side: on the left half, in Ibn Battuta’s time, a few visitors and yogis move around; on the right half, centuries later, the lower walls are buried in bushes and young trees, with no figures in sight.

dialogue.text: His brief notice is one of the last clear voices from medieval Kajarra. After him the record thins, but the stone stayed, while forest and politics shifted around it.

i18n.hi: उसका यह छोटा ज़िक्र मध्यकाल के ‘कजार्रा’ की आख़िरी साफ़ आवाज़ों में है। उसके बाद लेख कम पड़ते जाते हैं, पर पत्थर वहीं रहे, जंगल और सियासत ही बदलती रही।

panels.shot: somber long shot of distant army and temples
panels.action: Far off on a hazy plain, an army standard bearing the name of Sikandar Lodi moves past, while, nearer in the frame, temple towers rise among trees, suggesting but not showing direct assault.

dialogue.text: Persian chronicles later speak of Sultan Sikandar Lodi’s 1495 campaign against temples in this region, including Khajuraho, but they do not name which shrines fell or what exactly was lost.

i18n.hi: फारसी इतिहासों में आगे चलकर सुल्तान सिकंदर लोदी के 1495 के मंदिर-विरोधी अभियान का ज़िक्र है, जिसमें खजुराहो भी आता है, पर कौन से मंदिर गिरे, क्या खोया, यह नहीं लिखा।

panels.shot: slow pan across overgrown temple base
panels.action: Thick creepers wrap the lower courses of a Khajuraho temple; small village shrines with fresh flowers nestle near the bigger, older plinth, smoke from a ritual fire drifting in the foreground.

dialogue.text: What is clear is slower: stone weathering, jungle pressing in, village worship adapting. Great mandapas cracked and filled with roots, even as smaller shrines nearby still woke with bells at dawn.

i18n.hi: जो साफ़ दिखता है, वह धीमा है: पत्थर घिसना, जंगल का चढ़ आना, गाँव की पूजा का बदलना। बड़े मंडपों में दरारें पड़ीं, जड़ों ने जगह भरी, पर पास के छोटे मंदिरों में भोर की घंटियाँ अब भी बजती रहीं।

panels.action: A moonlit scene centuries later shows villagers gathered with lamps before a smaller shrine near the temple; in the background, the dark silhouette of Khajuraho’s main tower looms, its outline familiar yet unlit.

dialogue.text: When Alexander Cunningham came in the nineteenth century, he would find that Shivaratri still drew pilgrims. Khajuraho was never wholly forgotten; its role had simply changed.

i18n.hi: उन्नीसवीं सदी में जब अलेक्ज़ेंडर कनिंघम आया, तो उसने पाया कि शिवरात्रि पर अब भी यात्री आते थे। खजुराहो कभी पूरी तरह भूला नहीं, बस उसका काम बदल गया था।

panels.action: T.S. Burt rides in an open palanquin or on horseback with sepoy escorts along a rugged track, a local guide pointing ahead toward a distant mass of trees hiding the temples.

dialogue.text: In 1838, Captain T.S. Burt of the Bengal Engineers followed local guidance through scrub and rock. He expected some ruins; he did not expect an entire forest of carved stone.

i18n.hi: 1838 में बंगाल इंजीनियर्स के कप्तान टी. एस. बर्ट स्थानीय लोगों के साथ झाड़ियों और चट्टानों के बीच निकले। उसे कुछ खँडहरों की उम्मीद थी; पत्थरों के पूरे जंगल की नहीं।

panels.shot: revelatory wide as Burt breaks through foliage
panels.action: Burt pushes aside branches at the edge of thick jungle to reveal, suddenly, the great shikhara of a Khajuraho temple rising above the canopy, its tiers caught in late-afternoon light.

dialogue.speaker: T.S. Burt
dialogue.text: Good God! How comes such a city of temples to be hidden here?

i18n.hi: हे भगवान! इतने मंदिरों का शहर यहाँ छुपा कैसे रह गया?

panels.shot: careful mid-shot of Burt examining sculpture
panels.action: Burt, hat in hand, stands on a worn platform, peering closely at an erotic sculpture framed by other deities and dancers, while a local villager watches his reaction with mild curiosity.

dialogue.text: His printed account in 1838 marvelled at the delicacy and boldness of the figures, and at the sheer number of temples clustered here, half-choked in creepers and dust.

i18n.hi: 1838 की उसकी छपी रिपोर्ट इन मूर्तियों की नर्मी और हिम्मत पर, और बेलों व धूल में घिरे इतने मंदिरों की भीड़ पर हैरान होती है।

panels.action: A composite view shows Burt sketching in a notebook, a draftsman taking measurements of a temple base, and another soldier clearing brush from a stairway, while villagers look on.

dialogue.text: From his notes and sketches, news of Khajuraho travelled to Calcutta and beyond. The temples moved slowly from local landscape into learned journals and maps of Indian antiquity.

i18n.hi: उसकी नोटबुक और रेखाचित्रों से खजुराहो की ख़बर कलकत्ता से आगे दुनिया तक पहुँची। मंदिर धीरे-धीरे गाँव के नज़ारे से निकलकर विद्वानों की पत्रिकाओं और भारत की पुरानी नक्शों में बसने लगे।

panels.shot: Cunningham-era wide shot with pilgrims and surveyors
panels.action: Alexander Cunningham and his assistants stand with measuring rods and plans near a temple, while in the same frame a line of village pilgrims carrying pots and offerings passes by.

dialogue.text: When Cunningham came in the 1870s as head of the Archaeological Survey, his report noted not only plinths and plans, but a living Shivaratri pilgrimage that still circled these ancient walls.

i18n.hi: जब सत्तर के दशक में कनिंघम पुरातत्व सर्वेक्षण के प्रमुख बनकर आया, तो उसने सिर्फ़ नींव और नक्शे नहीं, बल्कि इन पुरातन दीवारों के चारों ओर घूमती जिंदा शिवरात्रि यात्रा भी दर्ज की।

panels.action: Modern ASI archaeologists in helmets and simple field clothes work carefully at Beejamandal, brushing soil from a massive buried plinth, while in the background another Chandela temple rises intact.

dialogue.text: Recent excavations at Beejamandal have exposed the base of a vast, long-lost temple nearby, reminding us that what we call the Khajuraho group is only part of a wider Chandela sacred landscape.

i18n.hi: बीजमंडल की हाल की खुदाइयों में पास ही एक विशाल, गुमशुदा मंदिर की नींव निकली है, याद दिलाती है कि जिसे हम ‘खजुराहो समूह’ कहते हैं, वह चंदेलों के बड़े पवित्र क्षेत्र का बस एक हिस्सा है।

panels.action: Delegates from different countries sit around a table with maps and photographs of Khajuraho; an Indian official gestures to a projected plan of the temple complex and buffer zones.

dialogue.text: By 1986, when UNESCO inscribed the Khajuraho Group of Monuments as a World Heritage Site, the conversation had widened again, from regional memory to global responsibility for stone left by the Chandelas.

i18n.hi: 1986 तक, जब यूनेस्को ने खजुराहो समूह को विश्व विरासत का दर्जा दिया, बात फिर फैल चुकी थी—स्थानीय याद से बढ़कर, चंदेलों के छोड़े पत्थर के लिए दुनिया की ज़िम्मेदारी तक।

panels.action: At twilight, the main Khajuraho temples glow under soft lighting; tourists with cameras, local priests, and a few pilgrims share the broad platform, while beyond them trees hide the darker forms of unexcavated mounds.

dialogue.text: From Ibn Battuta’s mutilated idols and yogis, through Burt’s startled sketches and Cunningham’s surveys, to today’s conserved plinths and ongoing digs, Khajuraho reminds us that what history neglects, careful hands and patient eyes can slowly recover.

i18n.hi: इब्न बतूता की टूटी मूर्तियों और योगियों से, बर्ट की हतप्रभ रेखाओं और कनिंघम की सर्वेक्षणों तक, और आज के सँवारे चबूतरों व चलती खुदाइयों तक, खजुराहो याद दिलाता है कि जिसे इतिहास छोड़ दे, उसे धैर्य भरे हाथ और चौकस आँखें धीरे-धीरे लौटा सकती हैं।

title_i18n.en: Khajuraho From Forest to World Heritage
title_i18n.hi: खजुराहो: जंगल से विश्व विरासत तक

subtitle_i18n.en: From Chandela dust to UNESCO stone, the long remembering of Khajuraho
subtitle_i18n.hi: चंदेलों की राख से यूनेस्को की शिला तक, खजुराहो की लंबी याद
